damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 254–255: When Dumbledore asks what the stolen objects are and why Riddle took them, Riddle says nothing that reveals warmth or need for connection. Dumbledore tells him to return them to their owners 'with your apologies.' Riddle does not look 'remotely abashed' and watches Dumbledore 'coldly and appraisingly.' The subsequent analysis (Book Scene 281) makes clear these are trophies of cruelty, souvenirs of power over victims — the 'magpie-like tendency' Dumbledore identifies as a key to understanding the Horcruxes.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 7, when Dumbledore asks 'Why did you want these things, Tom?', Riddle answers: 'I like having things that belonged to other people. It makes me feel... close to them.' This is an invented line not present in the book corpus. It reframes trophy-collecting as a manifestation of loneliness and longing for connection rather than predatory dominance and the desire to possess trophies of victimisation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This rewrite is directly damaging because Dumbledore's analysis of Voldemort's magpie-like trophy-collecting is the foundation for understanding why he chose the specific objects he turned into Horcruxes. The film's substitution — loneliness rather than predatory domination — makes Voldemort more sympathetic and obscures the link between his childhood cruelty and his later choices. It also misrepresents the psychology of a character Dumbledore explicitly describes as incapable of love or genuine connection.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Orphanage) — Mrs. Cole's gin-drinking scene and her detailed account of Riddle's history are cut
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 207–219: Mrs. Cole gives Dumbledore a detailed account over gin — the girl who arrived and died, Riddle's naming, the rabbit hanging from the rafters, Amy Benson and Dennis Bishop being 'never quite right' after the cave visit. Dumbledore uses gin and charm to extract this; the scene establishes both the method (flattery and social intelligence) and the content (a catalogue of childhood sadism escalating in seriousness). Her final comment — 'I don't think many people will be sorry to see the back of him' — is significant characterisation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6 cuts directly to the corridor and Mrs. Cole mentions only that Tom is 'odd' and there have been 'nasty things' with other children, giving no specific examples. There is no gin, no extended account, no detail about the rabbit or the cave children. The film moves immediately to Riddle's room.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The specific incidents Mrs. Cole describes in the book — particularly the cave visit — are directly relevant to the cave sequence later in the film. Their absence means the cave's emotional and narrative weight (Riddle terrorising children here as a boy) is only stated by Dumbledore in a single line rather than shown to have been established by witness testimony. It also removes texture from young Riddle's portrait of escalating, calculated cruelty.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Orphanage) — Riddle's demand that Dumbledore prove himself and his commanding tone are softened
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 227–232: Young Riddle says 'I don't believe you' with 'ringing force,' speaks the words 'Tell the truth!' as 'a command,' and later says 'Prove it' 'at once, in the same commanding tone.' When Dumbledore says he won't force him to come, Riddle sneers 'I'd like to see them try.' The book stresses that Riddle already behaves like someone accustomed to exerting power over others.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7 has Riddle say 'I don't believe you. I hear Mrs. Cole talking...' in a measured, contained way, and 'Prove it' as a flat statement. The confrontational commands ('Tell the truth!', the sneer about seeing them try) are absent. Riddle is more watchful and still than imperious and commanding.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's young Riddle already displays the instinct to dominate and issue commands — he has 'given it many times before.' This is a deliberate early marker of Voldemort's core personality. The film's Riddle is more passively menacing (staring, stillness, spiders) which is atmospheric but loses the specific quality Dumbledore later identifies: Riddle's contempt for authority and his compulsion to be obeyed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Orphanage) — Riddle does not go alone to Diagon Alley; the exchange about his father's identity is cut
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 257–271: Riddle says bluntly 'I didn't have any money' (without thanks for the money bag), insists 'I don't need you. I'm used to doing things for myself,' and then, just as they are about to part, 'as though it burst from him in spite of himself,' asks 'Was my father a wizard?' Dumbledore notes he had 'withheld mention of this strangest power until that moment, determined to impress' with the Parseltongue revelation. These beats show self-sufficiency, suppressed need, and the nascent obsession with paternal identity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7 ends with Riddle revealing Parseltongue and Dumbledore departing, but the entire exchange about going alone to Diagon Alley and Riddle's question about his father is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The question about his father — erupting involuntarily despite Riddle's careful self-control — is one of the few moments in the books where Voldemort's suppressed human wound is visible. Dumbledore's later analysis of Riddle's obsession with his parentage (Book Scenes 321–322) is partially unmoored without this seed. The self-sufficiency detail also reinforces the 'operates alone' trait Dumbledore flags as key to understanding the Horcrux strategy.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12 / Scene 17 (Slughorn Horcrux memory, both corrupted and true versions) — The true memory omits Riddle's visible greed and the specific question about seven
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 538–559: The true memory (obtained by Harry) shows Riddle's 'hunger' becoming 'apparent' and his expression becoming 'greedy, he could no longer hide his longing.' When Riddle asks about splitting the soul more than once and specifically proposes 'isn't seven the most powerfully magical number,' his face at the end is described as showing 'wild happiness... the sort of happiness that did not enhance his handsome features, but made them, somehow, less human.' Slughorn is shown genuinely regretting the conversation and 'gazing at Riddle as though he had never seen him plainly before.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 17 includes the key content (the seven question, Slughorn's horror) but Riddle's physical tells of naked greed and the description of his face becoming 'less human' with happiness are not conveyed — the film presents him as controlled throughout, only turning away to look in a mirror with a hint of red in his eyes. Slughorn's moment of truly seeing Riddle for the first time is not dramatised.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of the true memory is important not only for the information content but for what it reveals about Riddle's mask slipping — a rare moment of unguarded hunger. The film's version preserves the plot but loses the characterisation: the sense that even at sixteen, Riddle was barely containing something monstrous behind his polished facade.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 18 (Dumbledore's Office after Horcrux memory) — Entire analytical framework about Voldemort's past, multiple Horcruxes, and specific objects is drastically compressed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 561–632: After seeing the true memory, Dumbledore delivers an extended analysis covering: the confirmed existence of multiple Horcruxes; that Riddle probably made six plus the seventh in his body; the locket and cup as likely candidates; the diary already destroyed; the ring already destroyed; Nagini as a probable Horcrux; the prophecy's true meaning (Voldemort created his own enemy); love as power; Harry's freedom of choice. This is a major expository and thematic scene spanning dozens of pages.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 18 compresses this to: seven Horcruxes confirmed; the diary and ring already identified; brief mention that they 'can be anything'; a flash of images (ring, cup, snake, derelict house) when Harry touches the ring; and Dumbledore saying he may have found another and asks Harry to come with him. The specific identifications of likely objects, the discussion of Nagini, the analysis of why Voldemort preferred Horcruxes to the Sorcerer's Stone, and the extended discussion of love and prophecy are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This compression significantly damages the audience's understanding of the Horcrux quest that will drive the entire next film. The book's scene is where Harry (and the audience) receives the intellectual and emotional framework for everything that follows: why these specific objects, how many, what has already been done, and what Harry's real power is. The film substitutes a brief visual montage and leaves most of the strategic and thematic content unspoken. The discussion of love as Harry's defining power — one of the saga's central themes — is entirely absent from the film corpus.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 18 — Dumbledore's reaction to learning Snape passed on the prophecy is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 636–642: Harry confronts Dumbledore with the revelation that Snape overheard the prophecy and reported it to Voldemort, leading directly to the deaths of his parents. Dumbledore's face whitens. Harry rages. Dumbledore defends Snape, saying Snape did not know which boy would be targeted, and that his remorse 'is the greatest regret of his life and the reason he returned.' Harry demands to know how Dumbledore can be sure, and Dumbledore says 'I trust Severus Snape completely.' This is a pivotal scene for Snape's arc and Dumbledore's relationship with Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This confrontation does not appear in the film corpus at all. The revelation about Snape and the prophecy, and Dumbledore's defence of him, are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is crucial for three intersecting arcs: Snape's hidden motivation (remorse over Lily's death), Dumbledore's trust in Snape (and the reason behind it), and Harry's justified fury. Removing it means audiences in the next film will lack the emotional and narrative groundwork for Snape's full revelation. It also removes a key beat in the Dumbledore-Harry relationship where Harry's anger is legitimate and Dumbledore's defence of Snape is costly.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (Cave) — Dumbledore's commentary on Voldemort's psychology during the cave sequence is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 648–671: Throughout the cave sequence, Dumbledore offers a running analysis of Voldemort's thinking — why the boat is sized for one wizard's power, why Voldemort didn't worry about a child's magic registering, why the island's poison won't immediately kill its victim (Voldemort wants information first), why Voldemort fears death and darkness while claiming superiority. Each observation illuminates Voldemort's psychology and his specific blind spots.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 19 presents the cave sequence as primarily physical and atmospheric. Dumbledore speaks about the blood toll at the entrance and briefly about the place 'knowing magic,' but the sustained psychological commentary about Voldemort's design choices, his fear of death, and his underestimation of youth is largely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the cave as a teaching moment — Dumbledore demonstrates his method of reading Voldemort's mind through the physical evidence of his defences. This models for Harry (and the audience) the kind of thinking needed to defeat Voldemort. Its absence means the cave is primarily spectacle rather than the penultimate lesson in Dumbledore's curriculum for Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 20 (Astronomy Tower) — Dumbledore's disarming and the tower confrontation with Malfoy is changed in a way that alters Dumbledore's agency
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus does not contain the tower scene in the excerpt provided, but Book Scene 678 references the tower events (Malfoy's boasts, Snape's vow, 'he'll slither back'). The book establishes that Dumbledore was immobilised by a Petrificus curse before being disarmed — he did not willingly allow Malfoy to Expelliarmus him. Harry, hidden and immobilised by Dumbledore's prior spell, could not act.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 20 shows Dumbledore deliberately and slowly drawing his wand ('without intent') as if to offer it to Malfoy, effectively inviting the Expelliarmus. Dumbledore appears to choose to be disarmed as a tactical or compassionate gesture toward Malfoy. Harry, hiding below, is not shown to be under any binding spell — he chooses to stay hidden on Dumbledore's instruction.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's version transforms Dumbledore from a man caught off-guard while already weakened into a figure making a deliberate, almost Christ-like surrender. While this is a valid interpretive choice, it removes Harry's anguish at being physically prevented from acting — in the book, Harry is bound by Dumbledore's spell and cannot intervene even if he wanted to. The film's Harry simply obeys an instruction, which is less dramatically devastating and removes the specific guilt of paralysis that the book creates.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 21 (Grounds chase) — Snape reveals he is the Half-Blood Prince during the chase
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 683–685: During the chase, Snape deflects Harry's spells and orders him not to use Occlumency against him ('Blocked again and again and again until you learn to keep your mouth shut and your mind closed, Potter!'). The revelation of the Half-Blood Prince identity does not occur during the chase in the book — it is discovered separately.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 21 has Snape reveal 'Yes. It's me. I'm the Half-Blood Prince' during the chase itself, as a parting taunt. This is a significant restructuring of when and how this revelation lands.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Moving the Half-Blood Prince revelation into the heat of the chase transforms it from a discovery Harry makes in grief and reflection into a villain's parting taunt. It reduces the quiet horror of realising the mentor figure of the annotated textbook was the same person who just killed Dumbledore, and converts a moment of complex irony into a melodramatic exit line. The emotional and thematic weight of the revelation is diminished.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Great Hall feast) — Dumbledore's speech about Voldemort is vague and brief; the deeper context established in the book is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 144: Dumbledore's feast speech in the book directly names Voldemort, emphasises the danger, and is described as making the 'silence seem to tauten and strain.' It is substantive and direct. The book corpus also establishes (Scenes 68–69) that Dumbledore had already spoken directly to the Dursleys about the open state of war and Harry's danger.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 has Dumbledore give a speech that mentions Tom Riddle's student days and warns that 'dark forces attempt to penetrate this castle,' but the central warning is diffuse and ends with the odd, deflating 'their greatest weapon remains... you' / 'Just something to keep in mind. Now, off to bed. Pip pip!' Ron comments 'That was cheerful' — the film itself flags it as an anticlimactic non-speech.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's Dumbledore frequently undercuts gravity with deflating humour ('Pip pip') in a way that slightly softens his authority and the seriousness of the threat. In the book, the feast speech carries genuine weight. This is a recurring pattern in the film's Dumbledore characterisation across this instalment — consistent with the broader criticism of the adaptation — but the corpus evidence for this specific scene supports a modest impact weight.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Death Eater meeting, opening) — Voldemort's tone toward Lucius re: wand exchange
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Voldemort publicly humiliating Lucius with cruel, malicious wit: 'Give you my wand, Lucius? My wand?' followed by sniggering from the throng, and a prolonged, sadistic interrogation about why the Malfoys look unhappy with his presence. The cruelty is deliberate, savored, and public.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film omits the mocking 'Give you my wand, Lucius? My wand?' exchange and the surrounding sniggering entirely. Voldemort's tone upon taking the wand is measured and businesslike. The sadistic public humiliation that establishes Voldemort's enjoyment of cruelty toward his own followers is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book Voldemort relishes degrading even his most loyal followers publicly; the film softens this into cold efficiency. The scene loses the portrait of a leader who enjoys cruelty for its own sake, which is a defining personality trait.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Death Eater meeting) — Bellatrix volunteers to kill Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book there is no such exchange; Bellatrix expresses devotion ('it is an honor to have you here') and Voldemort teases her about family news (Tonks/Lupin marriage), demonstrating his manipulative control over even his most fanatical follower. The book Voldemort enjoys toying with Bellatrix's emotions.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film adds a line where Bellatrix volunteers to kill Harry ('I'd like to kill the boy'), and Voldemort rebuffs her by explaining the twin-core problem. This is invented film dialogue that shifts Voldemort's explanation of the wand problem from a general announcement to a response to Bellatrix.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but the film's Voldemort here is reactive rather than controlling the room entirely on his own terms. The book's Voldemort never needs prompting; he dictates the agenda entirely.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Death Eater meeting) — Pius Thicknesse present and addressed by Voldemort
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not have Thicknesse present at the meeting. Voldemort asks Yaxley about the Ministry takeover timeline and engages in a strategic discussion about when Scrimgeour can be surrounded. The meeting focuses on Snape/Yaxley intelligence rivalry and Voldemort's cool strategic thinking.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film inserts Thicknesse into the meeting as a present participant, whom Voldemort calls on ('Pius, what say you?') and compliments ('Spoken like a true politician. You will prove most useful'). This compresses exposition but invents a scene beat not in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor structural compression. The book's more extended strategic discussion reveals more of Voldemort's patience and political cunning; the film shorthand slightly flattens this.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Death Eater meeting) — Charity Burbage execution: Voldemort's tone and speech
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Voldemort a lengthy, contemptuous speech about Burbage: 'Not content with corrupting and polluting the minds of Wizarding children, last week Professor Burbage wrote an impassioned defense of Mudbloods...' with ideological conviction and building anger. 'Nobody laughed this time. There was no mistaking the anger and contempt in Voldemort's voice.' He silences Burbage with a wand flick mid-plea.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Voldemort delivers a shorter, more measured and almost civilized version: 'We can agree to disagree.' His tone is ironically polite rather than oozing contempt. The ideological fury of the book speech is replaced with cold sarcasm.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes that Voldemort's genocidal ideology is not merely strategic but genuinely felt and expressed with passion. The film's ironic 'we can agree to disagree' reduces this to a pose, slightly undermining the ideological horror of the character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Malfoy Manor cellar) — Ollivander torture scene replaces book version
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Voldemort's torture of Ollivander through Harry's scar-vision: Harry feels Voldemort's 'surge of vicious anger' and sees 'the white hand raise its wand' while Ollivander writhes. The scene is experienced through Harry's empathic scar connection, establishing the mental link as a source of horror and intelligence.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows the Ollivander scene directly (not through Harry's scar-vision), with Voldemort as a visible silhouette at the top of stairs, threatening Ollivander about the broken wand. The framing removes the scar-connection dimension entirely and presents it as a straightforward scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this moment to develop both the scar-connection as Harry's involuntary window into Voldemort's cruelty and Voldemort's frustrated fury at wand failure. The film loses the subjective horror of Harry experiencing Voldemort's anger from inside.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 25 (Grindelwald's cell) — Voldemort confronts Grindelwald
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus establishes (through Dumbledore's later explanation in King's Cross) that Grindelwald tried to stop Voldemort going after the wand, lied and pretended he had never had it — potentially an act of remorse. The book does not dramatize this scene directly in the corpus but Dumbledore says: 'Perhaps that lie to Voldemort was his attempt to make amends.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film dramatizes the scene: Grindelwald taunts Voldemort ('You're so innocent, Tom. Like a schoolboy') and ultimately tells him the wand is buried with Dumbledore. He does not lie to protect it. The film Grindelwald cooperates (eventually) rather than attempting to misdirect Voldemort as the book implies.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Grindelwald-lie is a moment of late redemption that Dumbledore finds meaningful. The film eliminates this by having Grindelwald lead Voldemort to Dumbledore's tomb, removing a subtle moral beat about redemption and love as forces even dark wizards can feel.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 26 (Dumbledore's tomb) — Voldemort's manner at the tomb
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book describes Voldemort approaching the tomb with 'controlled euphoria,' 'a sense of purpose and power and rightness,' and 'triumph' — entirely cold and goal-focused. 'He raised the old yew wand: How fitting that this would be its last great act.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Voldemort momentarily 'transfixed by the sight of his old foe at peace' and the moment of claiming the wand is described as 'oddly tender' — he covers Dumbledore's hands with his own before taking the wand.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Voldemort feels nothing but triumphant purpose at Dumbledore's tomb. The film's 'oddly tender' moment implies some residual feeling toward his old enemy — a humanization not supported by the book, which explicitly states he had 'no sadness in him, no remorse' even when killing Snape. This misrepresents Voldemort's complete incapacity for emotional connection with those he has defeated.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 29/30 (Malfoy Manor, post-Gringotts) — Voldemort's rage at learning Horcrux was taken
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives an extended, devastating interior view of Voldemort's reaction: frenzied disbelief, mass killing of goblins and witnesses, stomping alone among the dead, and then a controlled reassessment as he methodically plans to check each Horcrux. The passage shows both his terror and his capacity to recover into cold logic: 'A modicum of calm cooled his rage now.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Voldemort killing goblins and guards in a rage with the Elder Wand, then speaking to Nagini in Parseltongue about checking on hiding places with a rapid flash of Horcrux images. The transition from frenzied rage to cold planning is much compressed and the interior anguish ('He was crazed, frenzied') is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's extended scene is one of the most revealing portraits of Voldemort's psychological vulnerability — his terror that his immortality strategy might be unraveling. The film compression loses the depth of his existential fear and the paradox of the most powerful dark wizard being secretly terrified.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scenes 49/50 (Boathouse) — Voldemort kills Snape
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Voldemort in the Shrieking Shack, not a boathouse. More significantly, the book's Voldemort delivers a full, extended soliloquy about the Elder Wand's failure, working through his reasoning aloud: 'I have thought long and hard, Severus... I believe that your wand imbibed some of the power... I have performed my usual magic. I am extraordinary, but this wand... no.' The scene is long, measured, and reveals Voldemort's methodical (if flawed) reasoning. He also says 'I regret it' coldly after killing Snape.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's boathouse scene is significantly compressed. Voldemort arrives already near the conclusion ('The Elder Wand cannot serve me properly, Severus, because I am not its true master... You killed Dumbledore, Severus. While you live, the Elder Wand cannot be truly mine'). The extended reasoning process is cut. The chilling 'I regret it' line from the book is absent; instead Voldemort says 'only I can live forever' and immediately commands Nagini.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's extended scene reveals Voldemort at his most intellectually engaged and most self-deceived — he genuinely believes his reasoning is sound. The film's compression removes the portrait of a brilliant but fatally limited mind working through a problem. The 'I regret it' line, present in the book, also shows his capacity for cold performative courtesy that makes him more uncanny.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 50 (Boathouse) — Voldemort's line 'only I can live forever'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Voldemort say: 'It cannot be any other way. I must master the wand, Severus. Master the wand, and I master Potter at last.' His motivation is mastery and conquest of Harry, not a statement about his own immortality being exclusive.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Voldemort say: 'You have been a good and faithful servant, Severus. But only I can live forever.' This reframes his motivation as a jealous monopoly on immortality rather than the specific wand-mastery logic.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Voldemort kills Snape as a logical (if wrong) step in mastering the Elder Wand to defeat Harry. The film's version makes it sound like Voldemort kills loyal servants simply because he cannot share immortality — a cruder, less intellectually interesting motivation that misrepresents his specific wand-logic obsession.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 56 (Forbidden Forest clearing) — Voldemort's address to Harry: 'Come to die'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's Voldemort in the forest clearing says only 'Harry Potter. The Boy Who Lived' very softly, with his head tilted 'like a curious child.' He is described as having frozen when Harry appeared, then staring with 'a singularly mirthless smile.' He raises his wand with his head still tilted 'considering the boy.' The tone is quiet, almost wondering.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film adds 'Come to die' to Voldemort's greeting ('Harry Potter. The Boy Who Lived. Come to die.'). This is an invention not in the book corpus for this scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The addition of 'Come to die' makes Voldemort sound like a theatrical villain announcing himself. The book's Voldemort in this moment is quietly, almost disturbingly controlled — his stillness and soft voice are more menacing than a taunt. The film line trades psychological menace for a crowd-pleasing villain flourish.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 61 (Courtyard procession) — Voldemort's speech about Harry's cowardice
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's Voldemort tells the assembled survivors: 'Harry Potter is dead. He was killed as he ran away, trying to save himself while you lay down your lives for him.' He uses the lie to demoralize, and also: 'He was nothing, ever, but a boy who relied on others to sacrifice themselves for him.' This is a calculated propaganda speech.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Voldemort deliver a much longer, more elaborate and almost poetic speech about Harry's absence during the battle: 'While your hands ran dark with the blood of mothers and sons... his were clasped in prayer — but it was a prayer for one and one only... he had long since fallen to his knees... he begged me for mercy in a voice as meek as a child's.' This is substantially invented rhetoric not in the book corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film invents an extended, almost rhetorically sophisticated demoralization speech. While Voldemort is intelligent, the book's version of this moment is cruder and more direct. The film's version makes Voldemort sound like a skilled orator, which somewhat contradicts the book's portrait of a man who has contempt for human emotional bonds and rarely bothers to perform empathy for crowds.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 57 (King's Cross) — Dumbledore's dialogue about the Hallows and his own failures
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's King's Cross scene includes Dumbledore's extensive explanation of wand mechanics, Voldemort's errors with blood magic, the Horcrux soul fragment, and a lengthy meditation on Dumbledore's own failures regarding the Hallows and Grindelwald. Crucially, Dumbledore explains: 'He was more afraid than you were that night, Harry... Your courage won.' And explains the twin-core wand phenomenon in detail.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's King's Cross scene omits the twin-core/wand-mechanics explanation entirely. It also omits Dumbledore's explanation that Voldemort's taking of Harry's blood in the graveyard created a two-fold connection that kept Harry alive ('He took into his body a tiny part of the enchantment your mother laid upon you'). The film Dumbledore says only that it was 'an educated guess' that Harry would survive, without explaining the blood-protection mechanism.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's King's Cross scene is where the audience learns why Voldemort's specific choices — taking Harry's blood, using the twin-core wand — turned against him. The film omits this, meaning Voldemort's defeat appears more arbitrary. This damages audience understanding of how Voldemort's own arrogance and ignorance of love-magic caused his downfall, which is a central saga theme.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scenes 62-72 (Final battle sequence) — Voldemort's extended duel with Harry through the castle
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's final confrontation between Harry and Voldemort takes place in the Great Hall, in front of all survivors, and consists primarily of a dialogue duel in which Harry methodically explains to Voldemort everything he got wrong: Snape's true allegiance, the Elder Wand's true master (Draco, then Harry), and offers Voldemort a chance at remorse. Voldemort's physical spells are described but the scene is dominated by Harry's words and Voldemort's increasingly destabilized responses. The killing curse rebounds when Voldemort fires and Harry uses Expelliarmus.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film replaces the stationary verbal confrontation with an extended physical chase-and-duel sequence through the castle, battlements, and courtyard, including Voldemort turning into smoke, wrapping Harry in his cloak, apparating repeatedly, and a physically grappling fall. The dialogue confrontation from the book ('You think you know more magic than I do?... You were wrong... Snape was Dumbledore's...') is compressed to a few brief exchanges on the battlements.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most structurally damaging deviation. The book's climax is fundamentally a battle of knowledge and moral understanding — Harry wins because he knows things Voldemort doesn't and understands truths Voldemort cannot grasp (love, loyalty, the mechanics of wand allegiance). The film replaces this with a physical spectacle chase. Voldemort's defeat in the film appears to be primarily a matter of physical combat and luck rather than Voldemort being undone by his own ignorance of love and loyalty. This directly undermines the saga's central theme that love and understanding defeat hatred and power. Harry's lengthy speech offering Voldemort remorse — one of the most morally significant moments in the series — is reduced to a taunt on the battlements.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 69/70 (Battlements) — Voldemort bleeds when Harry strikes him
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not include any moment where Voldemort bleeds from a physical blow in the final confrontation. The emphasis is entirely on magical contest and dialogue. Voldemort's mortality is demonstrated through the rebounding of his own curse.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Harry physically punch/strike Voldemort across the cheek, causing Voldemort to bleed visibly. Voldemort reacts with shock at the blood. This is invented for the film.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While minor in isolation, this moment physically humanizes Voldemort in a way the book deliberately avoids until the very end when he falls as 'just' a man. The book's Voldemort is made mortal by the rebounding of love-magic, not by a fist. Having him bleed from a punch earlier cheapens the symbolic significance of his death as a consequence of his own moral failures.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 72 (Final courtyard) — Voldemort's death: physical disintegration vs. simple fall
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book: 'Tom Riddle hit the floor with a mundane finality, his body feeble and shrunken, the white hands empty, the snakelike face vacant and unknowing.' His death is deliberately ordinary — he falls like a normal man. 'Voldemort was dead, killed by his own rebounding curse.' The mundane finality is the point.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Voldemort's body disintegrate into ash-like fragments that disperse into the air as he dies, a visually spectacular dissolution rather than a simple fall.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's 'mundane finality' is thematically essential — Voldemort, who feared death above all things and built an entire architecture of Horcruxes to escape it, dies as simply as any man. The spectacular disintegration in the film gives his death a grandeur that contradicts the book's deliberate deflation of the moment. It makes Voldemort's end feel appropriately cinematic rather than appropriately humbling.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 51 (Boathouse) — Ron's reaction to Voldemort's ceasefire announcement
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book after hearing Voldemort's announcement, Harry thinks about his situation; Ron does not shout a defiant response to Voldemort's voice in the air.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Ron bellow 'Never! Do you hear me! NEVER!' at Voldemort's disembodied voice after the ceasefire announcement.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor — this is more a Ron characterization issue than a Voldemort one, but it does dilute the weight of Voldemort's announcement by having it immediately countered with a shout rather than the stunned, heavy silence the book conveys.
